newsitem.title: CUBA: In unusual move, Cuban TV broadcasts parts of mass.
newsitem.headline: In unusual move, Cuban TV broadcasts parts of mass.

text.p: In an extremely unusual gesture, Cuban state television on Monday broadcast brief extracts from an open-air mass held on Sunday in the square in front of Havana Cathedral.

State television's lunchtime news programme showed about one minute of footage from the late afternoon service, which was led by Cardinal Jaime Ortega and attended by several thousand Roman Catholics. Cubans said they could not remember the last time any footage of a Catholic mass in Cuba was broadcast on state television.

The mass was the first open-air religious service to be held on the communist-ruled island in more than three decades and marked the start of preparations for Pope John Paul's visit to Cuba in January next year.
The service was held on the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul, founders of the church in Rome.
State television noted that the Havana mass was held outside because the cathedral is being renovated ahead of the papal visit.
Last week, church officials said they had asked the government for one of the papal masses to be broadcast live on state television during the visit.
The church also has asked for Ortega and other Cuban bishops to be able to appear on television ahead of the trip to explain the significance of the visit to Cubans.
These requests form part of the church's aim of achieving a wider place for the church in Cuba, including some access to the state-controlled media.
The national domestic agency AIN published a brief item on Sunday's mass, and the official news agency Prensa Latina, which serves both Cuban and foreign media, issued two reports on the service.

The most extensive coverage Cuban media has given of church issues was last November when President Fidel Castro met the pontiff at the Vatican. The papal visit was agreed to at that meeting, which marked a clear improvement in relations between the authorities and the church in the past year.

In the early 1960s, after Castro's 1959 revolution, church schools were nationalised and many foreign priests sent home. Christmas stopped being a public holiday. While there is now more tolerance for religion, religious practice remains limited to church premises.
